notes.meaning: Solomon started building the temple exactly 480 years after the Israelites left Egypt, during the fourth year of his rule. The work began in the month of Ziv, which is in the spring. This fixed date shows that building a permanent house for God was a major turning point in Israel's history.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view 480 years as a symbolic figure of twelve forty-year generations and date the Exodus later, to the 1200s BC.

notes.meaning: The main building was about ninety feet long, thirty feet wide, and forty-five feet high. Its design followed the floor plan of Moses' tent sanctuary, the tabernacle, but doubled its size. While not huge compared to some ancient palaces, it was built with the finest materials to honor the Lord.

Solomon added an entrance porch across the front of the temple on the east side. It was thirty feet wide to match the width of the main hall, and it stuck out fifteen feet. Worshippers entered through this grand entryway into the holy place.

The temple was fitted with high, narrow windows made with wooden frames. These openings let fresh air in and allowed smoke from the lamps and incense to drift out. Because they had fixed lattices, people outside could not look in.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The windows were placed in the main hall for ventilation and incense smoke, while the Most Holy Place remained completely dark.

notes.meaning: Solomon built a three-story complex of side rooms along the outside walls of the temple. The rooms became wider on each higher floor because the stone walls were made thinner in steps. The wooden beams rested on these stone ledges so that no holes had to be cut into the main temple walls.

Every stone was shaped and dressed at the rock quarry before it was brought to the building site. As a result, no hammer, chisel, or iron tool made any noise while the temple was going up. This reverence showed that God's holy house was built with quiet order rather than human clamor.

The doorway to the side rooms was placed on the south side of the building. A winding stairway went up from the ground floor to the middle level, and another went up to the top story. Priests used these private stairways to reach storage spaces and workrooms.

Solomon finished the outer structure of the temple and roofed it with sturdy cedar beams and planks. He wrapped the outer walls with the three levels of side rooms, each about seven and a half feet high. These side chambers rested on the cedar supports that lined the building.

While construction was underway, the Lord sent a personal message to Solomon. God likely spoke through a prophet to guide and encourage the young king. This divine word reminded Solomon of what truly mattered in God's eyes.

God promised to keep His covenant with David and to dwell among the Israelites if Solomon obeyed all His commands. The Lord made it clear that a magnificent building could never replace heartfelt obedience to God's law. Even the most costly house could not keep God's blessing if the king turned away from Him.

Encouraged by the Lord's promise, Solomon kept working until the entire temple was completed. He did not quit halfway through the demanding project. True dedication to God means finishing the work He gives us to do.

Solomon covered the inside stone walls with cedar wood from the floor to the ceiling. He also paved the bare floor with smooth cypress boards. This careful work gave the interior of the house a warm, rich appearance.

A cedar partition was built thirty feet from the back wall to create the Most Holy Place, also called the inner sanctuary. The larger room in front was the Holy Place, which was sixty feet long. These dimensions created two distinct rooms, just like the tabernacle had before.

Carvers decorated the cedar paneling with patterns of wild gourds and blossoming flowers. The wooden lining covered every wall completely, so not a single rough stone was visible inside. The design mirrored the beauty and life of God's creation.

Solomon prepared the inner room to hold the ark of the Lord's covenant, the sacred chest that showed God was with His people. This room formed a perfect cube of thirty feet on each side, completely overlaid with pure gold. Solomon also covered the incense altar in front of it with cedar and gold.

Solomon covered the entire inside of the temple with gold and placed gold chains across the entrance of the inner room. The altar of incense beside the entrance was also gilded. Everything was finished with the greatest possible beauty to honor God's holy presence.

Inside the Most Holy Place, Solomon placed two giant cherubim sculpted from wild olive wood, each fifteen feet tall. The wings of the first cherub were each seven and a half feet long, giving it a total wingspan of fifteen feet. These winged heavenly guardians watched over the sacred space.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars compare these cherubim to the winged sphinx-like figures often depicted in ancient Near Eastern royal and religious art.

notes.meaning: The second cherub was identical in shape, height, and wingspan to the first. Both figures stood fifteen feet tall on the floor of the inner room. Their matching size gave a balanced and awe-inspiring appearance to the sacred shrine.

Solomon set the two cherubim side by side in the inner sanctuary with their wings stretched out wide. One wing touched the north wall, another touched the south wall, and their inner wingtips touched in the middle of the room. He then overlaid both wooden figures with pure gold.

Carvers etched figures of cherubim, palm trees, and flowers across the walls of both the inner and outer rooms. Solomon also covered the wooden floors of both rooms with plates of gold. The gold and garden carvings pointed to God's holiness and reminded worshippers of Eden.

For the doorway into the Most Holy Place, Solomon built two folding doors out of olive wood with decorative doorposts. The doors were carved with cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers, and then coated with hammered gold. These beautiful doors formed the entrance to God's throne room.

The entrance to the main hall was made with olive-wood frames and folding doors of cypress wood. These doors were also carved with cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers, with thin gold hammered neatly over the woodwork. The folding design let the doors open easily while still keeping the room grand and dignified.

Solomon built a low wall around the inner courtyard using three layers of cut stone topped by a layer of cedar beams. This court was reserved for the priests who served at the bronze altar and the washbasins. The low wall allowed the rest of Israel to look in and watch the worship from the outer yard.

The temple foundation was laid in the spring month of Ziv during Solomon's fourth year as king. The entire complex was completed down to the last detail in the autumn month of Bul during his eleventh year. The building took seven and a half years to complete, showing both the careful planning and the earnest labor put into God's house.
